### READING COMPREHENSION I
Read the following passage carefully, and answer the questions that follow

The Moon has been worshipped by primitive peoples and has inspired humans to create everything from lunar calendars to love poems, but what do we really know about it? The most accepted theory about the origin of the Moon is that it was formed of the debris from a massive collision with the young Earth about 4.6 billion years ago. A huge body, perhaps the size of Mars, struck the Earth, throwing out an immense amount of debris that came together and cooled in orbit around the Earth.

The development of Earth is closely related to the moon; the Moon’s gravitational influence upon the Earth is the primary cause of ocean tides. In fact, the Moon has more than twice the effect upon the tides than does the Sun. The Moon makes one rotation and completes a revolution around the Earth every 27 days, 7 hours, and 43 minutes. This simultaneous rotation is caused by an uneven distribution of mass in the Moon (essentially, it is heavier on one side than the other) and has allowed the Earth’s gravity to keep one side of the Moon permanently facing Earth. It is an average distance from Earth of 384,403 km.

The Moon has no atmosphere; without an atmosphere, the Moon has nothing to protect it from meteorite impacts, and thus the surface of the Moon is covered with impact craters, both large and small. The Moon also has no active tectonic or volcanic activity, so the erosive effects of atmospheric weathering, tectonic shifts, and volcanic upheavals that tend to erase and reform the Earth’s surface features are not at work on the Moon. In fact, even tiny surface features such as the footprint left by an astronaut in the lunar soil are likely to last for millions of years, unless obliterated by a chance meteorite strike. The surface gravity of the Moon is about one-sixth that of the Earth’s. Therefore, a man weighing 82 kilograms on Earth would only weigh 14 kilograms on the Moon. The geographical features of the Earth most like that of the Moon are, in fact, places such as the Hawaiian volcanic craters and the huge meteor crater in Arizona. The climate of the Moon is very unlike either Hawaii or Arizona, however; in fact the temperature on the Moon ranges between 123 degrees C. to –233 degrees C.

What is the passage primarily about?

options.A: the Moon’s effect upon the Earth
options.C: what we know about the Moon and its differences to Earth
options.D: a comparison of the Moon and the Earth
options.E: how the ocean tides get influenced by The Moon

explanation_steps: The passage provides a comprehensive overview of the Moon, covering its origin, its physical relationship with Earth (tides and rotation), its lack of atmosphere and volcanic activity, and comparing its surface and gravity to Earth. Therefore, it is about general knowledge of the Moon and how it differs from Earth.

Therefore, when used responsibly, technology serves as the ultimate tool for progress and human empowerment.

### Reading Passage I

Learning a second language is always a good thing. For those who do make the effort to acquire a second language, whether as children or later on as adults, the process can yield brain-boosting benefits— regardless of the level of fluency achieved. Research suggests that it's a good idea to introduce the second language as early as possible, as children learn the sound and rhythm of their birth language at a very young age. Parents can expose their child to two languages in different ways.

When I was seven years old, I went to a school for the first time. While there, we were all encouraged to write letters back home. I wrote a detailed letter in English to my mum, telling her about all the activities we were doing. I then translated the letter word for word into Dutch for my dad, a native Dutch speaker. This story still makes my dad, who is fluent in both Dutch and English, laugh.

My parents raised my sisters and I bilingually from birth. They sought advice and were told to only speak their respective languages to us. They stuck to this so strictly that for an embarrassingly long time we did not realize that they both spoke Dutch and English fluently. Nowadays, we speak a Dutch-English blend at home, often switching between languages mid-sentence.

There is also another strategy that can work well for parents who speak different languages. The parents could speak to their child in a different language each day of the week. This is sometimes referred to as “time and place” strategy among language experts. The families may associate each language with specific time or location. The whole family might be speaking one language on weekends or over shared meals, for example, and another language during the week, or when they are outside their home.

Other parents may choose to speak just one language at home, often a minority language, as they know their child will be exposed to the other language outside the home. In the US and UK, for example, Spanish would be a minority language and English, the majority language. Migrant families from Spain in those countries may choose to speak to their kids in Spanish at home and the children will be exposed to the majority language outside their home. In addition, the migrant families may need to make a special effort to keep the minority language going, especially once the children become more independent. Otherwise, it is generally more at risk of fading away in children’s lives as their interactions outside the home increase, and the majority language becomes more dominant. Generally, parents can apply any one of these different approaches to raise bilingual children. The most effective strategies are those that can be incorporated consistently and long-term. The strategy that will be successful is the one that works for your particular family and makes the experience enjoyable and not a chore.

51. Fill in blank **51** with the correct verb form.
explanation_steps: The context is 'last night' (past). The 'main road' is singular. The road didn't flood itself; it was flooded by the rain (passive voice). Therefore, 'was + V3' (was flooded) is correct.

questions.stem: 52. Fill in blank **52** with the correct verb form.
explanation_steps: 'People' is a plural subject. Like the previous blank, this is a passive construction in the past tense: the people didn't force someone else; they were forced by the situation. 'Were forced' is the correct plural past passive.

questions.stem: 53. Fill in blank **53** with the correct modal verb.
explanation_steps: The sentence is in the past tense. 'Could' is the past form of 'can', used here to express ability in the past ('whatever they could gather' - ዝኸኣልዎ ክእክቡ) .

Abdu: Guess what! **54** to Massawa.
Matewos: Really. When?
Abdu: Tomorrow. I am flying with Eritrean Airlines.

54. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **54**.
explanation_steps: Abdu is talking about a fixed plan for the future ('Tomorrow'). In English, the Present Continuous tense ('I am going') is frequently used to describe confirmed future arrangements.

questions.stem:
Matewos: **55** to the airport?
Abdu: No, thanks. I can get a taxi.

55. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **55**.
explanation_steps: Abdu's answer 'No, thanks. I can get a taxi' implies that Matewos offered him transportation. 'Do you need a ride?' is the standard way to offer someone a lift in a car.

questions.stem:
Matewos: ...There are many **57** historical places that you can visit.
Abdu: **56**
Matewos: Yes. Several times.

56. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **56**.

options.A: When will you go to Massawa?
options.B: When have you gone to Massawa?
options.C: When did you go to Massawa?
options.D: Have you ever been to Massawa?

explanation_steps: Matewos answers 'Yes. Several times.' This type of answer (Yes/No + frequency) is a response to a question about life experience, which uses the Present Perfect: 'Have you ever been...?'

questions.stem: 57. Fill in blank **57** with the correct form of the word.
explanation_steps: The blank comes before the noun 'places'. We need an adjective to describe the places. 'Interesting' is the adjective form used to describe things that cause interest.

questions.stem:
58. Natnael: You didn't come to school yesterday, did you?
Salman: __________.
explanation_steps: In English, if you are confirming a negative question/tag ('You didn't...'), you must use a negative answer ('No, I didn't') to agree that you indeed did not go. Choice B is the correct way to confirm absence.

questions.stem: 59. Adiam: Hana, you hardly attended the meeting last week, ________?
explanation_steps: The word 'hardly' makes the sentence negative. Negative sentences require a **positive question tag**. Since the verb 'attended' is in the simple past, the auxiliary verb for the tag is 'did'. Thus, 'did you?' is correct.

Semira: Hi Saba.
Saba: Hi Semira.
Semira: How are you?
Saba: I’m fine, thank you. What about you?
Semira: **60**.

60. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **60**.
explanation_steps: All the options (A, B, C, D) are common, polite, and grammatically correct ways to respond to 'What about you?' or 'How are you?' in a friendly conversation.

Semira: ...Where have you been all these days?
Saba: **61**
Semira: How was it then?

61. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **61**.

options.B: I have been on a trip
options.C: My uncle was not feeling well
options.E: You have been on a tour

explanation_steps: Semira asks 'Where have you been?' and then follows up with 'How was it?'. The pronoun 'it' suggests Saba was at a place or event. 'I have been on a trip' (B) provides the location/activity that Semira is asking about in the next sentence.

questions.stem:
Semira: How was it then?
Saba: **62**

62. Choose the best alternative to fill in blank **62**.

options.C: I had best moments of my life

explanation_steps: Semira is asking for Saba's opinion on her trip. All the provided options (A, B, C, D) are positive, appropriate, and common ways to describe a good experience or trip. Therefore, 'All of the above' is correct.

questions.stem: 63. **Sentence:** This file must be saved in hard disc.

options.A: Hard disc must save the file.
options.B: We must save the file in hard disc.
options.C: This file was saved in hard disc.
options.D: We saved the file in hard disc.

explanation_steps: The original sentence is in the passive voice ('must be saved'). To change it to active, we need a logical subject (like 'we' or 'you') and the active modal form 'must save'. Option B maintains the same tense and meaning.

questions.stem: 64. **Sentence:** Many tourists visit the historical site Adulis every year.

options.A: Many tourists are visiting the historical site Adulis every year.
options.B: The historical site Adulis was visited by many tourist every year.
options.C: Many tourists were visiting the historical site Adulis every year.
options.D: The historical site Adulis is visiting by many tourist every year.
options.E: The historical site Adulis is visited by many tourist every year.

explanation_steps: The sentence is in the Simple Present active ('visit'). To change it to passive, we use 'am/is/are + V3'. Since 'the historical site Adulis' is singular, we use 'is visited'. Option E is the correct passive construction.

questions.stem: 65. **Sentence:** Nejat was selected by the committee to be secretary of the company.

options.A: The committee selects Nejat to be secretary of the company.
options.B: Nejat selected the committee to be secretary of the company.
options.C: The committee was selected Nejat to be secretary of the company.
options.D: The committee selected Nejat to be secretary of the company.
options.E: The committee had selected Nejat to be secretary of the company.

explanation_steps: The sentence is in the Simple Past passive ('was selected'). Its active equivalent is the Simple Past 'selected'. The subject (the committee) must perform the action in the active voice.

questions.stem: 66. **Sentence:** Someone was cleaning the room.

options.A: The room is cleaned by someone.
options.B: Someone had been cleaning the room.
options.C: The room was being cleaned by someone.
options.E: The room was cleaned by someone.

explanation_steps: The sentence is in the Past Continuous active ('was cleaning'). The passive form for continuous tenses must include the word 'being'. The structure is 'was/were + being + V3'. Thus, 'was being cleaned' is correct.

questions.stem: 67. **Indirect:** She asked me whether I had seen the film.

options.A: She asked me, “Did you see the film?”
options.B: She asked me,” Do you see the film?”
options.C: She asked me, “Whether did I see the film?”
options.D: She asked me, “Had I seen the film?”
options.E: She asked me, “Did I see the film?”

explanation_steps: The reported speech uses 'had seen' (Past Perfect), which usually comes from the Simple Past ('Did you see?') in direct speech. The word 'whether' indicates it was a Yes/No question in direct speech.

questions.stem: 68. **Direct:** He said to me, “What are you doing?”

options.A: He said to me what are you doing.
options.B: He asked me what you are doing.
options.C: He asked me what I was doing.
options.D: He asked me what you were doing.
options.E: He said to me what was I doing.

explanation_steps: In reported speech: 1. 'Said to me' becomes 'asked me'. 2. Present Continuous 'are doing' becomes Past Continuous 'was doing'. 3. The pronoun 'you' changes to 'I' because he is talking to me. 4. The word order changes from question to statement.

questions.stem: 69. **Direct:** They said, “We were going to the stadium.”

options.A: They said that they were going to the stadium.
options.B: They said that we were going to the stadium.
options.C: They said that they had been going to the stadium.
options.D: They said that they went to the stadium.
options.E: They said that we are going to the stadium.

explanation_steps: Past Continuous ('were going') in direct speech changes to Past Perfect Continuous ('had been going') in indirect speech. The pronoun 'we' changes to 'they'.

questions.stem: 70. **Indirect:** She said that she would see me the next day.

options.A: She said, “You could see me tomorrow.”
options.B: “you would see me the next day,” she said.
options.C: She said, “You will see me tomorrow.”
options.D: “I will see you tomorrow,” she said.
options.E: She said that she will see you tomorrow.

explanation_steps: To go from indirect to direct: 1. 'would' becomes 'will'. 2. 'the next day' becomes 'tomorrow'. 3. 'she' becomes 'I' in the quote. Choice D correctly matches these transformations.

### Reading Passage II

Not since the end of the colonial era has any one nation had such a wide as well as deep influence on Africa as China. This profound change has happened over so short a period. Those who are critical of the China-Africa relationship, especially the West, view the presence of China in the continent as having a hidden agenda.

The Chinese arrival in Africa, unlike previous incursions, was not led by gunboats. Instead, they politely knocked on the door and when leave to enter was given, they came in with smiles, firm handshakes and an overflowing abundance of goods and the means— financial as well as technical— to provide Africa with what it needed most— a stream of infrastructure. It was an offer that no sensible could refuse. And the Chinese companies, unlike others, did not just make pledges, they delivered immediately. The Chinese want resources to build their own economy and Africans need plenty of cheap goods and lots of infrastructure.

Despite the fact that China is now the second-largest economy in the world, it is still a developing country that has moved more of its citizens out of poverty more quickly than any other nation has done in history and wants the same for Africa. China itself remembers what it was like to be a colony of foreign powers and no one can deny that it was a staunch supporter of Africa’s liberation struggle.

In addition, its economic logic is faultless. Its spectacular rise has been built on making things and trading them. It needs trading partners and you cannot trade with a poor nation. So if you can help other nations to become more prosperous by building their infrastructure, you also become more prosperous by trading with them. For the past two decades, the goods on sale throughout Africa are made in China.

The number of Chinese in Africa seems to multiply by the week. Some of them pop up in all sorts of places, engaging in different business activities. That is one picture of the Chinese in Africa. The other is the massive construction and infrastructure project sweeping right across the continent. The hallmark of Chinese construction projects has been speed— speed of decision, speed of funding and speed of execution— all at relatively cut-price cost.

As far as trade is concerned, Chinese buyers are gobbling up virtually anything on sale in Africa— minerals, oil, gas, cotton, leather, tea, coffee and foodstuffs. Going in the other direction are hundreds of thousands of containers crammed full of manufactured items— ranging from toys and textiles to all sorts of electronic devices.

Generally, the Chinese are engaged in all kinds of economic activities. There are more than 10,000 Chinese-owned firms operating in Africa today. Nearly a third are involved in manufacturing, a quarter in services, and around a fifth in trade and in construction. All these firms are having a positive impact on Africa’s economic growth.

71. According to the information in paragraph 2, Africa needs

options.A: trade and investment to develop its economy.
options.C: to import raw materials for industries.

explanation_steps: In paragraph 2, the text mentions that the Chinese provided 'financial as well as technical' means and a 'stream of infrastructure'. It explicitly states that 'Africans need plenty of cheap goods and lots of infrastructure'. This translates to a need for trade and investment to develop the economy.

questions.stem: 72. What is the motive of China in Africa?

options.A: It wants to settle part of its large population in Africa.
options.B: It wants the resources of Africa.
options.C: It wants to have some colonies.
options.E: It wants to get jobs to the poor.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 2 directly answers this: 'The Chinese want resources to build their own economy'. This identifies Africa's natural resources as a primary motivation.

questions.stem: 73. How does the writer compare the Chinese and the others in terms of completing projects?

options.A: The Chinese finish projects in time.
options.B: The others don't promise at all.
options.C: The Chinese are fast in decision only.
options.D: The Chinese are slow in accomplishing projects.
options.E: The Chinese are fast in funding projects.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 5 highlights 'speed' as the hallmark of Chinese projects, specifically mentioning 'speed of decision, speed of funding and speed of execution'. Option E directly matches one of these specific attributes mentioned in the text.

questions.stem: 74. Which business activity has the largest share?
explanation_steps: The last paragraph provides the statistical breakdown: 'Nearly a third (1/3) are involved in manufacturing, a quarter (1/4) in services, and around a fifth (1/5) in trade and in construction.' 1/3 (approx 33%) is the largest portion among the given fractions.

questions.stem: 75. According to the information in the passage, China

options.C: has moved more citizens out of poverty.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 3 explicitly mentions all these points: China is the 'second-largest economy' (B), yet still a 'developing country' (A), it has 'moved more of its citizens out of poverty' (C), and it 'remembers what it was like to be a colony' (D).

questions.stem: 76. Which items are imported from China to Africa?
explanation_steps: Paragraph 6 explains the direction of trade. Minerals, oil, cotton, and coffee go **from Africa to China**. Manufactured items like 'toys and textiles to all sorts of electronic devices' go **from China to Africa**.

questions.stem: 77. The general message of the writer is that the

options.B: relationship between Africa and China is a win-win situation.
options.C: Chinese are more beneficiary in Africa.
options.D: Chinese are increasing unemployment in Africa.
options.E: Chinese are dominating the business activities of Africa.

explanation_steps: The writer portrays the relationship as mutually beneficial: China gets resources it needs, and Africa gets 'what it needed most' (infrastructure) and cheap goods. The text concludes that these firms are having a 'positive impact on Africa’s economic growth'. This implies a 'win-win' situation.

questions.stem: 78. **Pledges**
explanation_steps: The text says companies 'did not just make pledges, they delivered immediately'. This contrasts words with actions. A pledge is a solemn promise or undertaking.

questions.stem: 79. **Staunch**
explanation_steps: The text calls China a 'staunch supporter of Africa’s liberation struggle'. In this context, it means a very loyal, firm, and committed supporter. 'Outstanding' is the closest positive adjective in the given options.

questions.stem: 80. **Spectacular**
explanation_steps: The text refers to China's 'spectacular rise'. This describes growth that is beautiful in a dramatic and eye-catching way, or very **impressive**.

**Directions:** Write a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph of about **200 words** on **ONE** of the following topics.

1. What makes a country attractive for tourists?
2. Why do some students excel in their academic performance?
questions.answer: Student chooses one topic and writes a 200-word paragraph.
accepted_answers: Student chooses one topic and writes a 200-word paragraph.
explanation_steps:
To write an excellent academic paragraph, follow these steps:
1. **Topic Sentence:** Clearly state your main idea in the first sentence.
2. **Supporting Details:** Provide 3-4 reasons or examples to back up your main idea.
3. **Transition Words:** Use words like 'Furthermore', 'In addition', and 'Consequently' to connect your thoughts.
4. **Concluding Sentence:** Summarize your points and restate your main idea in a new way.
5. **Word Count:** Aim for approximately 200 words as requested.

### READING COMPREHENSION I

**Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow.**

The world is facing a food crisis. The prices of grains in general and wheat in particular, and vegetable oil have soared on the international market. The World Food Programme (WFP) warned in April that 2022 would be a terrible year of hunger. Soaring food prices and supply shortages have pushed 44 million people in 38 countries to the edge of famine.

Several factors are responsible for the current global food crisis. Thanks to the vast mechanization of agriculture which resulted in low cost of grain production, developed countries managed to sell grain to developing countries in large amounts cheaply. **This is undermining** agriculture in developing countries. For decades, global food prices have been dominated by few companies, which control a large percentage of grain trade around the world.

Developed countries' use of grain for industrial purposes is also squeezing global food supply. According to a current research, 36 percent of corn produced in the United States is used to produce ethanol. Forty-one percent of soybean produced in the United States and 20 percent of that produced globally are used to make biodiesel. Sixty-four percent of rapeseed in the European Union and 20 percent of that produced globally are also used for biodiesel.

In recent years the world has been shaken by the COVID-19 pandemic, extreme weather and geopolitical conflicts. In 2020 and 2021, Brazil saw severe droughts and a **slump** of soybean production, while south Asia was ravaged by rainstorms, which resulted in declining rice and palm output. Russia and Ukraine are major wheat producers and exporters, so the clash between them disrupted the global supply chain. And this disruption has sent global wheat price to stratospheric level, resulting in a 40 percent rise in wheat price.

Moreover, food waste in some developed countries must be blamed for the food crisis. In the United States, for example, discarded food amounts to 150,000 tons every day, 12 percent being grain and 39 percent vegetables and fruits. In addition, thirty million acres of cultivated land remain unharvested each year, wasting several million tons of grain.

Amid the **intensifying** global food crisis, food security – a situation in which people can have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food – has become an issue of greater concern. Therefore, the world should work together to find a solution for this crisis. Only through global cooperation can we keep in check the current food crisis and ensure food security for the world's population.

Which one of the following statements **is true** according to the information in the reading text?

options.A: 44 million people died because of the rise in food prices.
options.B: WFP warned that there would be hunger in April.
options.C: Few companies have dominated the global grain trade.
options.D: FAO warned that there would be hunger in April 2022.

explanation_steps: According to the second paragraph, 'For decades, global food prices have been dominated by few companies, which control a large percentage of grain trade around the world.' This directly supports option C.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 the writer said, '**This** is undermining agriculture in developing countries.' What does the word '**This**' refer to in the passage?

options.A: The rise in global food prices
options.B: Grain being sold to developing countries cheaply
options.C: Modernization of agriculture in developed countries
options.D: The high cost of exporting grain

explanation_steps: The word 'This' refers to the preceding sentence: 'developed countries managed to sell grain to developing countries in large amounts cheaply.' This cheap selling makes it hard for local farmers in developing countries to compete.

questions.stem: According to paragraph two, what is the contribution of agricultural mechanization to grain production?

options.A: It increased the cost of production of grain.
options.B: It decreased the cost of production of grain.
options.C: It affected developed countries' agriculture negatively.
options.D: It enabled developing countries to export grain at lower price.
options.E: It motivated farmers in developing countries to produce more.

explanation_steps: The text states: 'Thanks to the vast mechanization of agriculture which resulted in **low cost of grain production**...'

questions.stem: The cause for the 40 percent increase in wheat price is
explanation_steps: Paragraph four mentions that Russia and Ukraine are major producers and the 'clash between them disrupted the global supply chain... resulting in a 40 percent rise in wheat price.'

questions.stem: One of the following **is not** the reason for the global food crisis.

options.A: Exporting grain to developing countries at low cost
options.B: Exporting grain to developed countries at low cost
options.C: The conflict between Russia and Ukraine

explanation_steps: The text mentions developed countries selling to *developing* countries cheaply (Choice A), which undermines local farming. It does not mention grain being exported to *developed* countries at low cost as a cause of the crisis.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, the United States is described as

options.E: a place where a large amount of food is wasted.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 5 highlights food waste, stating that in the United States, 'discarded food amounts to 150,000 tons every day.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following could be the best title for the passage?
explanation_steps: The entire passage discusses the various causes, effects, and potential solutions related to the current world food crisis. While other options (A, C, D) are mentioned, they are only sub-topics.

questions.stem:
For items 8-10, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.

**Undermining**
explanation_steps: In the context of the text, cheap imports are hurting or 'weakening' the local agriculture of developing countries.

questions.stem: **Slump**
explanation_steps: The text mentions Brazil saw 'severe droughts and a slump of soybean production.' Droughts cause production to drop or fall.

questions.stem: **Intensifying**
explanation_steps: The text speaks of the crisis getting worse or 'growing' in severity.

questions.stem: Saron hasn't finished _________ the assignment on the computer **yet**.
explanation_steps: The verb **'finish'** is always followed by a **gerund** (-ing form) when another verb follows it.

questions.stem:
**Teacher:** You haven't done the homework today, _________?
**Student:** No, I'm afraid not.
explanation_steps: When the main sentence is **negative** ('haven't done'), the question tag must be **positive** ('have you').

questions.stem: Listen to those people, what language _________?
explanation_steps: The word 'Listen' indicates an action happening **now**. Therefore, we use the **Present Continuous** tense ('are they speaking').

questions.stem: The match between the two rival teams _________ fascinating. Everyone enjoyed it.
explanation_steps: The subject is **'The match'** (singular). Since the second sentence ('enjoyed') is in the past tense, the first verb must be the singular past form **'was'**.

questions.stem: My younger brother is good at tennis. He plays tennis _________.
explanation_steps: We need an **adverb** to modify the verb 'plays'. 'Good' is an adjective, and **'well'** is its corresponding adverb.

questions.stem: **Ali:** Well, I studied it in school and I've been having private tutorial classes _________ last summer.
explanation_steps: We use **'since'** to refer to a specific point in time in the past when an action started ('last summer').

questions.stem: When I was waiting for the bus at the bus stop, the man next to me _________ chatting.
explanation_steps: The sentence describes an action that interrupted or happened during another past action. The interruption is expressed in the **Simple Past** ('started').

questions.stem: Which sentence is **correctly** capitalized and punctuated?

options.A: The secretary told me “the windows are not locked.”
options.B: The director told the students, “The exam starts at 08:30am.”
options.C: She said “The electric bill reading is 62:80 nakfa.”
options.D: The invigilator asked, “Do you all have admission cards?”
options.E: My father asked me, “where are you going”

explanation_steps: Option D follows all rules: a comma after the reporting verb, opening quotation marks, a capital letter for the start of the quote, and a question mark inside the quotation marks.

questions.stem: My sister _________ next month. I will go to the wedding with my family but my younger brother can't come.
explanation_steps: The **Present Continuous** ('is getting married') is commonly used to describe fixed future arrangements or plans.

questions.stem: _________ of our understanding of computers has come in the past twenty years of study.
explanation_steps: 'Understanding' is an **uncountable** noun. **'Much'** is the quantifier used for large amounts of uncountable things.

questions.stem: This is a non-smoking area. Could you ________ your cigarette, please?
explanation_steps: The phrasal verb **'put out'** means to extinguish a fire or a cigarette.

questions.stem: Most high school students want ________ expository and descriptive paragraphs.
explanation_steps: The verb **'want'** is followed by a **to-infinitive** (to + verb).

questions.stem: The loan application ________ by the bank because it hadn't been filled out properly.
explanation_steps: The sentence describes a completed action in the past where the subject (the application) received the action. This requires the **Simple Past Passive** ('was' + past participle).

questions.stem:
**Abdu:** ________ about this event?
**Idris:** Nobody told me. I read it in the newspaper.
explanation_steps: When asking about the subject of a sentence (who did the action), we don't use the auxiliary verb 'did'. The correct form is **'Who told you?'**

questions.stem: The grandmother was ________ the children while their parents were out for business.
explanation_steps: The phrasal verb **'looking after'** means taking care of someone or something.

questions.stem:
**Abraham:** Where's Daniel? I think all of us should have been here half an hour ago.
**Azieb:** He ________ lost. It isn't easy to find this place.
explanation_steps: To express a possibility about a past event, we use **'might have' + past participle** ('might have got').

questions.stem: I had my camera with me in Massawa last month ________ photographs.
explanation_steps: The word **'but'** is used to show contrast. Having a camera is expected to result in taking photos; not taking any is a contrast.

questions.stem:
For items 28-32, choose the alternative that is most similar or close in meaning to the given sentence.

**If the bus hadn't been late, I would have arrived on time.**

options.A: The bus was late, but I arrived on time.
options.B: The bus was late, so I didn't arrive on time.
options.C: The bus wasn't late, so I arrived on time.
options.D: The bus isn't late, so I arrive on time.
options.E: The bus wasn't late, so I didn't arrive on time.

explanation_steps: This is a **Third Conditional** sentence ($$ If + had + P.P, would + have + P.P $$). It describes a hypothetical past. The reality is the opposite: The bus **was** late, and I **didn't** arrive on time.

questions.stem: **Although he studied hard, he failed the exam.**

options.A: In spite of his studying hard, he passed the exam.
options.B: Because he didn't study hard, he failed the exam.
options.C: In spite of his studying hard, he failed the exam.
options.D: Because of his studying hard, he passed the exam.
options.E: Despite his studying hard, he passed the exam.

explanation_steps: **'Although'** and **'In spite of'** both express contrast (concession). Option C correctly maintains the original meaning: hard study + failure.

questions.stem: **Alex doesn't mind having lots of work.**

options.B: He doesn't like lots of work.
options.C: He doesn't dislike having lots of work.
options.E: A and C are possible answers.

explanation_steps: If you **'don't mind'** something, it means you don't dislike it (Choice C). In many contexts, it also implies you are happy or 'like' to do it (Choice A).

questions.stem: **If I don't call my mother, she'll start worrying about me.**

options.A: Unless I call my mother, she'll start worrying about me.
options.B: I should call my mother. Otherwise, she'll start worrying about me.
options.C: I will call my mother, so she'll start worrying about me.
options.D: I will not call my mother, so she'll not start worrying about me.
options.E: A and B are possible answers.

explanation_steps: Both A and B carry the same meaning as the original sentence. 'Unless' means 'if not', and 'otherwise' indicates what will happen if the first condition (calling) isn't met.

questions.stem: **He didn't manage to get out.**

options.A: He wants to get out and he does.
options.B: He wanted to get out and he did.
options.C: He wanted to get out but he couldn't.
options.E: He was able to get out.

explanation_steps: 'Manage to' implies attempting something and succeeding. Therefore, 'didn't manage to' implies he tried/wanted to do it but failed (couldn't).

questions.stem:
**For items 39-45, choose the preposition that best fits the context from among the alternatives given below.**

options.B: My friend told me, "I had a job interview yesterday."
options.C: My friend told me, "I had been in a job interview yesterday."
options.D: My friend told me, "He has a job interview yesterday."
options.E: My friend told me, "I was having a job interview yesterday."

explanation_steps: In indirect speech, **Past Simple** ('had') changes to **Past Perfect** ('had had'), and **'yesterday'** changes to **'the previous day'**. Working backwards, 'had had' becomes 'had'.

options.B: Saron said to Semira, "I wanted to become an electrical engineer."
options.C: Saron told Semira, "I want to become an electrical engineer."
options.D: Saron said to Semira, "I want to become an electrical engineer."
options.E: Saron told Semira, "She wanted to become an electrical engineer."

options.B: The director asked the students if you all were going to the picnic.

### READING COMPREHENSION II

**Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow.**

Picture children playing games of football on major urban streets. Tourists stood in the middle of the street nonchalantly taking photos. Restaurants spilling out onto small squares – and not a car or bus in sight.

Such are my memories of Venice, the only car-free city I have ever been to, when I and my friend visited during a student summer holiday. The Italian city is, of course, unique in that it is built on a series of small islands– yet it is a refreshing experience being able to wander around without **dodging** in and out of traffic.

For the last 100 years, the car has come to dominate the urban landscape. Streets have been widened in many cities to accommodate automobiles, and huge amounts of space are given over to parking them. Private vehicles have revolutionized mobility, but they have also introduced many ills, from pollution to traffic accidents.

And today some cities are trying to design the car out of the urban landscape altogether. Both Oslo in Norway and the Spanish capital Madrid have made headlines in recent years for banning cars from their centers– although neither has entirely got rid of them yet. Their moves toward this, however, represent a broader **trend** in cities to make driving more difficult. Similarly, in one part of Mexico City, for example, you drive on different days depending on whether your license plate ends in an odd or even number.

There is also an environmental aspect. Oslo is built in a geological bowl, which during winter in particular, causes the city to suffer from serious air pollution problems. Data from the local government shows a marked decline in air pollution over the past decade. There has also been a drop in trips made by car– from 35% of journeys in 2009 to 27% in 2018– with a parallel rise in people either walking or using bicycles or public transport.

Besides the well-documented problems of air pollution and the millions of deaths caused by traffic every year, the largest effect cars have on society is the tremendous damage they do to social spaces. Cars significantly reduce social interaction. The places that are most popular in cities are always the spaces with no cars. They may be parks, squares or **pedestrianized** areas. In some USA cities as much as 70% of urban land is given over to parking. Today's housing crisis stems from a lack of land. Get rid of cars and the problem is solved immediately.

Opponents of this plan argue that removing cars would be helpful to reduce pollution and could improve public health. But if you take away cars from people, you need to be able to provide an alternative good public transport.

In one newly built city, everything is walkable. There are high number of intersections which make it very easy to get around by foot or bicycle. There are also vertical connectivity, with bridges between high rises. The Great City, which is designed to house 100,000 people, is only one square kilometer across and it would never take more than 10 minutes to walk from one point to another.

What is the reason behind Mexico City’s introduction of driving on different days depending on the car’s plate number?

options.B: It is to increase the number of cars on the streets.
options.C: It is to reduce fuel consumption.
options.D: It is to discourage people driving.

### The Importance of Giving Awards to High Scoring Students

Recognizing academic excellence through awards and prizes is a vital component of a successful educational system. Firstly, awards serve as a powerful motivator. When students know that their hard work and late-night study sessions will be acknowledged publicly, they are more likely to push their boundaries and strive for excellence. This healthy competition encourages everyone in the classroom to improve their performance, raising the overall academic standard of the school.

Secondly, prizes provide students with a sense of accomplishment and self-worth. High school can be a challenging period, and receiving a tangible reward for one’s effort builds confidence, proving to the student that dedication leads to success. This boost in morale often carries over into other areas of life, fostering a 'can-do' attitude that is essential for future career challenges. Moreover, awards can sometimes offer practical benefits, such as scholarships or books, which further aid a student’s educational journey.

Finally, honoring high achievers sets positive role models for younger learners. When junior students see their seniors being celebrated for their intellect and discipline, they are inspired to follow in their footsteps. In conclusion, giving awards is not just about the prize itself, but about fostering a culture of meritocracy, hard work, and continuous self-improvement within the youth.
